digest.definition: The fields study cultural and communicative activity as a central force in economic, political, psychological and social life, and how people make, share and read meaning
distinctiveFeatures: The fields study cultural and communicative activity as a central force in economic, political, psychological and social life, and how people make, share and read meaning

They draw on the arts, humanities and social sciences and on creative and professional practice in the cultural, film and communication industries, with links to design, business, marketing and computing
A broad family of courses with varied emphases, from theory and history to production and professional practice, under many titles; the statement is a framework, not a prescription

Eleven shared propositions bind the courses: culture and media shape lives, identities and power, are major employers, are unequally open to participation and call for informed debate on their politics, law and ethics
Courses combine understanding and skills in different measures, often with practice used to inform critique or critique to inform practice
The fields have a long record of critiquing inherited hierarchies of power and representation, and the statement casts teaching staff as agents of change
Courses commonly engage students in the three Cs of media literacy: cultural access, critical understanding and creative activity
The fields are agile, responding quickly to new technologies and practices, generative AI among them

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: the fields' long critique of power and representation makes EDI part of the subject itself; the statement asks for EDI in every course and process, active recruitment, a diverse curriculum beyond tokenism, critical dialogue on gender, race, class, disability and colonialism, and an inclusive discipline as a student outcome at every rung (D1, 1.13 to 1.18, 3.7 to 3.12, 3.16)

headed Accessibility: emotional, functional and technical access built into design, delivery and assessment; reasonable adjustments, attainment gaps, accessible resources and a pedagogy of care, repeated in the EDI section (D1, 1.19 to 1.21, 3.10)

headed Sustainability: sustainability as a lens for course design, UNESCO's eight competencies, media representation of sustainability and the industry's own climate impact, ESD across the curriculum, the SDGs, BAFTA albert and sustainable studios and equipment; global issues and sustainable practice appear as student outcomes (D1, 1.22 to 1.30, 3.17)

headed Employability, enterprise and entrepreneurship education, and again Developing entrepreneurship and enterprise skills: careers in fast-changing creative industries, the economic weight of the sector, enterprise content such as intellectual property and production finance, enterprise for inclusion and sustainability, and entrepreneurial skills at every rung (D1, 1.31 to 1.33, 2.15, 3.13 to 3.17)

subjectSpecific.text: Depending on your course, you will be able to set what you learn in its historical, political, global, social, economic, cultural, environmental and technological settings.
Depending on your course, you will be able to grasp how social groups overlap and how groups and individuals take up and engage with media and communication in different ways.

Depending on your course, you will be able to judge critically when understanding, making and evaluating relevant forms, contexts and scenarios, and show how the knowledge and skills of the degree apply in real professional settings.
Depending on your course, you will be able to weigh and evaluate your own work reflexively against academic or professional codes, conventions, issues and debates.
You will usually be able to engage critically with the field's leading thinkers and arguments and put them to good use.
You will usually be able to understand how forms of communication, media, film and culture arose over time and how social, cultural, environmental and technological change shaped them.
You will usually be able to pursue sustained, independent, critical enquiry and research.
You will usually be able to frame research questions or lines of enquiry that feed into practice.
You will usually be able to choose, use and evaluate research methods that fit the context and the problem being researched.
You will usually be able to find, retrieve, judge and use data, sources and conceptual frameworks that suit research, production and professional practice in your own area.
You will usually be able to use the strengths, and know the limits, of fitting quantitative or qualitative methods, and apply this critically in your own work.
You will usually be able to show sensitivity to the subjective positions and intersections of different cultures, your own included, knowing that research and production are never neutral.
You will usually be able to show imagination and creative insight that suit the context.
You will usually be able to show awareness of, or attention to, sustainable ways of working.
You will usually be able to find, understand, criticise and keep to the ethical codes of relevant subject and industry bodies and to research standards.
You may be able to bring critical understanding to the ethical, culturally responsible use of media and cultural forms, practices and technologies of every kind, at work and in daily life.
You may be able to express yourself through communication, media, film and culture in ways shaped by cultural, media, digital and information literacies.
You may be able to appraise critically the social, cultural and political debates that bear on communication, media, film and culture.
You may be able to understand media and cultural policies and how they are made and put into effect.
You may be able to think about how varied communities and organisations can help shape media and cultural policy and practice.
You may be able to analyse how community and participatory media and communication feed cultural and political debate and challenges to power.
You may be able to think about global sustainability practice and debate as they bear on communication and cultural forms.

transferable.text: You will usually be able to analyse well and work through problems that may be theoretical, practical or professional.
You may be able to build the confidence to take part as responsible, informed citizens.
You may be able to stay open to varied discussion and debate in which others may question your own informed views and lived experience.
You may be able to work flexibly, creatively and independently, aware of ethical issues, directing yourself and reflecting on what you do.
You may be able to communicate well with others in person, sensitive to cultural difference and open to knowledge, ideas and approaches new to you.
You may be able to gather, order and use ideas and information to build clear arguments and put them across well in writing, speech, non-verbal, visual or other forms.
You may be able to find and produce information and judge sources when doing independent research.
You may be able to plan and run supervised projects that you direct.
You may be able to work well in a group or team, listening, contributing and leading well at different times.
You may be able to produce work to a set length, format, brief and deadline, citing sources and ideas properly and solving problems where that helps.
You may be able to use entrepreneurial skills, where they fit, with audiences, users, clients, consumers, markets or sources.
You may be able to build the information literacy to find and judge suitable sources and evidence with an eye to cultural context and sensitivity.
You may be able to engage critically with a range of media practices and competences.

You may be able to see that communication technologies, practices and products are never neutral but take shape in their social, cultural, economic, historical, environmental and geographical settings.
You may be able to look into career openings to get ready for possible jobs.
